Where is Omaha, and how do its neighborhoods differ?

Omaha is the largest city in Nebraska and the seat of Douglas County, along the Missouri River about 10 miles north of where the Platte River joins it. The 2020 census counted 486,051 residents, and the wider eight-county Omaha and Council Bluffs metro area, which crosses into Iowa, holds roughly one million people.

Neighborhood names carry real meaning to buyers here. Districts include Downtown, Midtown, North Omaha, South Omaha, West Omaha, East Omaha, the Old Market, Aksarben Village, Dundee, Benson, Florence, Little Bohemia, Bemis Park and Field Club. Housing age, size and condition vary from one of these districts to the next.

A seller in Dundee and a seller in West Omaha are working with very different houses, so any cash offer or listing price should be based on the street and the building, not on a citywide average.

What is the history behind Omaha's housing stock?

Omaha was founded in 1854 by land speculators from Council Bluffs, Iowa, around a river crossing called Lone Tree Ferry, which gave the city its nickname, the Gateway to the West. In 1898 it hosted the Trans-Mississippi Exposition, a world's fair that put the young city in front of a national audience.

Railroads and meatpacking drove the next century. Omaha became a national transportation hub in the 1800s, and in the 1900s the Omaha Stockyards, once the world's largest, and its meatpacking plants gained international prominence. A city that has grown steadily since the 1850s has housing from many eras, and owners of the oldest properties are often the ones asking whether a house that needs roof, foundation, plumbing or electrical work can sell as it stands.

Which employers keep Omaha's housing market moving?

Omaha's economy leans on insurance, banking, transportation, construction and health care. Four Fortune 500 companies have their headquarters here: Berkshire Hathaway, Kiewit Corporation, Mutual of Omaha and Union Pacific. Other Omaha-based names include First National Bank of Omaha, Gallup, Green Plains, Valmont Industries, Werner Enterprises and WoodmenLife.

  • Offutt Air Force Base, a large federal presence in the metro area
  • CHI Health, Methodist Health System and the Nebraska Medical Center
  • The University of Nebraska Medical Center
  • Omaha Public Schools
  • Hy-Vee and First National Bank of Omaha

Military and health care jobs bring frequent transfers and relocations. A family with orders or a new position elsewhere often has a fixed closing date, and that deadline is one reason owners in Omaha look at a direct sale instead of waiting for a lender-approved buyer.

How does Omaha weather affect a house and its sale?

Omaha sits in tornado country, and its record includes the Easter Sunday tornado of 1913 and the 1975 Omaha tornado outbreak. The city has also seen extreme temperatures, from a record low of minus 32 degrees Fahrenheit on January 5, 1884 to a record high of 114 degrees on July 25, 1936.

For a homeowner, that range puts steady stress on roofs, siding, windows, gutters and mechanical systems. A buyer's insurance company may ask about roof age. If you have an open claim or unrepaired storm damage, tell the buyer early, because insurance paperwork and unfinished repairs can complicate a closing.

The Missouri River shapes flood questions for low-lying parts of the metro area. Whether a particular address sits in a mapped floodplain is shown on FEMA flood maps, and a lender will require flood insurance when it does.

What does Omaha require of rental property owners?

Omaha runs a Rental Registration and Inspection Program, and it applies to anyone who leases a residential property for periods longer than 30 days inside the city limits or within three miles of its jurisdiction. It covers single-family houses, duplexes and apartments.

  • It is unlawful to offer a rental dwelling for lease, or continue leasing it, unless the property has been registered with the city.
  • Registration began on January 1, 2020.
  • Properties not on the annual inspection list go on a ten-year cycle, with one inspection between 2022 and 2032 and another every ten years after that.
  • The city lists a fee of $125 per rental dwelling or unit for each annual or ten-year inspection.
  • Questions go to 402-444-5150 or rentalregistration@cityofomaha.org.

If you are selling a rental, ask whether the property is registered and when it was last inspected, since a buyer or title company may raise it. Separate from the rental program, Planning Department Housing Enforcement handles complaints about deteriorated roofs and gutters, vacant and open structures, peeling paint, broken windows, inoperable vehicles in yards and similar conditions. Complaints are taken at 402-444-5371, extension 2070, or at enforceomaha@cityofomaha.org. An open complaint file is worth resolving before you sell.

How are Douglas County property taxes billed and appealed?

Douglas County property taxes are due by December 31, and the Treasurer mails statements every December. The key difference from many Nebraska counties is the delinquency calendar, which falls earlier in the year.

The Douglas County Assessor holds preliminary estimated value meetings before the formal protest period, and the state says counties with at least 150,000 residents send preliminary valuation change notices by January 15. If you disagree with the final value, you can file with the county Board of Equalization, which accepts protests online or on paper through June 30.

For a seller, the practical step is to ask the title company how the current year's tax will be split at closing, and to confirm that no earlier balance is open.

What does it cost to transfer a deed in Omaha?

The main transfer cost is Nebraska's documentary stamp tax, collected by the Douglas County Register of Deeds when the deed is recorded. The Department of Revenue states the rate is $3.32 for each $1,000 of value, or fraction of that, for deeds recorded on or after July 18, 2026, and that the tax falls on the grantor who executes the deed.

On a $300,000 house the tax is $996. Certain transfers are exempt, and the department publishes a list of exemptions, so check it for gifts, estate transfers and family deeds. A Real Estate Transfer Statement, Form 521, accompanies the deed. Recording fees are set by statute and the register's office posts its schedule.

Which school district serves Omaha homes?

Omaha Public Schools calls itself Nebraska's largest school district, and many city addresses fall inside it. Other districts serve parts of the Omaha area, so a buyer should confirm the district for a specific address before assuming anything.

OPS asks new families for proof of address, such as a utility statement, mortgage statement or rental agreement dated within three months. Students are assigned to a neighborhood school, and the district's placement office handles school choice requests. We do not rate schools, so use the district's own school search and a call to placement for a definite answer.

What do Omaha sellers typically run into?

Omaha sellers who consider a cash sale often have an inherited house in an older neighborhood, a rental that has not been inspected, a property with a housing enforcement complaint, or a deadline tied to a job transfer. Each has a clear next step: gather the deed and tax records, check the rental registration status, resolve any city notices, and decide whether repairs make financial sense.

A direct sale skips the lender's appraisal and loan approval, so the timeline depends mostly on title work and your readiness to sign. You can request a written offer, compare it to your other options and decide without any obligation.

When are Douglas County property taxes delinquent?

Taxes are due December 31. The first half becomes delinquent April 1 and the second half August 1, so payments should be in by March 31 and July 31. Nebraska law charges 14 percent annual interest on overdue balances.

Do I have to register a rental house in Omaha before I sell it?

If you lease a residential property for more than 30 days at a time inside Omaha or within three miles of its jurisdiction, city rules say it must be registered. Ask the Planning Department at 402-444-5150 whether yours is registered and when it is due for inspection.

What is the Nebraska deed tax on an Omaha sale?

The Department of Revenue lists $3.32 per $1,000 of value for deeds recorded on or after July 18, 2026, paid by the grantor. A $250,000 sale produces $830, unless the transfer is exempt.

How do I dispute my Omaha property valuation?

File a valuation protest with the Douglas County Board of Equalization between June 1 and June 30. Talking to the Assessor first, including at the preliminary value meetings, may resolve the issue without a formal protest.

What kind of city is Lincoln, Nebraska, for a home seller?

Lincoln is the state capital and the county seat of Lancaster County, and it is the second-largest city in Nebraska. It covers about 104 square miles, so the age, lot size and condition of a house vary a great deal from one part of town to another.

The city began in 1856 as the village of Lancaster, was renamed for Abraham Lincoln, and became the capital in 1869. The current state capitol was finished in 1932. Lincoln does not sit on the Platte or the Missouri. It was laid out near Salt Creek and the flat saline wetlands of northern Lancaster County, and the land rolls more as you move out from the center (Wikipedia).

The Lincoln metropolitan area is Lancaster County plus Seward County, and the combined area with Beatrice has about 372,000 residents by a 2024 estimate.

Which employers shape housing demand in Lincoln?

State government, the school district and the University of Nebraska-Lincoln are the largest employers in the city, with health care, finance and manufacturing behind them. The Lincoln Partnership for Economic Development lists Lincoln Public Schools and the University of Nebraska at 5,000 to 7,500 employees each, and names Nelnet, Ameritas, BNSF Railway, Duncan Aviation and Kawasaki Motors Manufacturing among other major employers (LPED).

The city's 2024 financial report, summarized on Wikipedia, ranks the State of Nebraska and Lincoln Public Schools in the 7,501 to 9,999 band, with the university next and Bryan Health fourth.

  • Government and education payrolls give the city a large base of salaried households.
  • Hospitals such as Bryan Health and St. Elizabeth Regional Medical Center add shift workers who may prefer to live near their jobs.
  • Sellers who relocate, inherit a house or divorce are among those who may want a faster closing than a listing offers.

How do Lincoln's neighborhoods and housing stock differ?

Lincoln has old and new areas side by side, and the age of a house usually decides what an inspector will flag. Several neighborhoods began as separate towns that the city annexed: Bethany in 1922, University Place in 1926, College View in 1929, Havelock in 1930 and West Lincoln in 1966. Historic districts sit near downtown, while newer subdivisions have grown mostly to the south and east.

Downtown housing has also grown. The same source reports about 1,200 downtown residents in 2010 and 3,000 in 2016.

Area typeTypical seller issue
Annexed former towns (Havelock, College View, University Place)Older wiring, plumbing and foundations on small lots
Historic districts near downtownDeferred exterior upkeep and rental conversions

What does Lincoln's climate mean for the roof, furnace and foundation?

Lincoln has a humid continental climate with cold winters, hot humid summers and thunderstorms that sometimes produce tornadoes. Snow averages 26 inches a season, and there are about 38 days a year with at least an inch on the ground. The average freeze-free window runs from April 25 to October 7, a growing season of 164 days (Wikipedia, citing NOAA).

Temperature swings are large. The city averages 41.8 days at 90 degrees or hotter and 10.1 nights at 0 degrees or lower, and it recorded minus 31 degrees on February 16, 2021.

Those swings are hard on shingles, gutters, concrete steps and older furnaces. A buyer's inspector will look at all of them. If yours are tired, a cash sale lets you skip the repair list and sell the house in its current state.

What local rules in Lincoln can affect a sale?

The biggest Lincoln-specific rule applies to buildings with three or more rental units, not to a typical single-family home. The city requires every owner of a property with three or more residential units to give a prospective buyer, at transfer, either a valid Certificate of Compliance or a notice of Minimum Housing Code deficiencies from the Building Official (City of Lincoln).

  • Fees listed by the city: $90 for the first three units, $12 for each additional unit, and a $70 fire inspection fee.
  • A certificate is valid for 90 days from issuance.
  • Inspectors check items such as roof structure, handrails, gutters, windows, smoke detectors and electrical safety.
  • If a buyer closes without a certificate, getting one becomes the buyer's job, and code deficiencies stay with the current owner.

Two other city programs matter to some sellers. A Neglected Building Registry covers vacant and neglected buildings. And since June 2021, a short-term rental license costs $250 per unit and renews every year, with a cap of 10 percent of units in multi-family premises in the R-1 through R-8 districts (City of Lincoln). If you run a listing on a house you plan to sell, check the license status first.

What does Nebraska require a Lincoln seller to disclose?

A Lincoln seller of a home with one to four dwelling units must give the buyer a signed written disclosure statement on or before the effective date of any binding purchase contract. Nebraska Revised Statute 76-2,120 sets that rule and lets a seller write "unknown" for anything outside personal knowledge (Nebraska Legislature).

The statement covers appliances, electrical, heating and cooling, water and sewer systems, hazardous conditions, title issues such as easements, and carbon monoxide alarm compliance. A buyer who is not given one can sue for actual damages, court costs and attorney's fees.

The statute lists exceptions. One matters for many Lincoln families: transfers by a fiduciary administering a decedent's estate are excluded unless the fiduciary lived in the home. Foreclosure sales and transfers between spouses or to lineal relatives are also excluded.

Who handles deeds and property taxes in Lancaster County?

The Lancaster County Assessor/Register of Deeds Office records the deed, and the County Treasurer bills and collects property tax. When a deed is recorded, Nebraska charges a documentary stamp tax on the seller. From July 18, 2026, the rate is $3.32 for each $1,000 of value or fraction of $1,000, up from $2.32 (Nebraska Department of Revenue). On a $200,000 sale that works out to $664, and a Real Estate Transfer Statement (Form 521) must be signed for the deed to be recorded.

Property tax is due each year on December 31. The Lancaster County Treasurer says state law allows two half payments without interest before the delinquent dates of April 1 and August 1 (Lancaster County Treasurer). A tax bill funds schools, the county, the city, fire districts and other local bodies, so it shows several levies.

At closing, the title company normally splits the current year's tax between you and the buyer. Ask for the parcel number early so you can check what has been billed.

How can a Lincoln seller choose between a listing and a cash sale?

The right choice depends on the condition of the house, how long you can wait and what you owe. A traditional listing may bring a higher price but adds showings, an inspection, repair requests and a financing contingency. A cash sale to a company like ours removes most of that, usually at a lower price.

  • Pick a listing if the house is in good shape and you can wait through a few months of showings.
  • Consider a cash sale if you inherited a house you do not want to repair, if tenants are in place, or if a move date is close.
  • Compare any offer against what a repaired and listed house would net after commissions, repairs and carrying costs.

Whichever way you go, get the parcel number from the Lancaster County Assessor/Register of Deeds records first, so you know exactly what the county has on file for the house.

More questions about Lincoln, NE

Do I need a Certificate of Compliance to sell my house in Lincoln?

Only if the property has three or more residential units. The city requires owners of those buildings to give the buyer a valid certificate or a deficiency notice at transfer. A single-family house is not described as needing one on the city's page.

How much is the Nebraska deed tax on a Lincoln home sale?

The documentary stamp tax is $3.32 per $1,000 of value for deeds recorded on or after July 18, 2026. The seller owes it, and the Lancaster County Register of Deeds collects it when the deed is recorded.

When are Lancaster County property taxes due?

Taxes are due December 31 each year. The County Treasurer lists April 1 and August 1 as the delinquent dates for the two half payments.

Do I have to give a disclosure statement if I sell for cash?

Yes, for a one-to-four unit home, unless a statutory exception applies. Nebraska law applies to residential sellers whether the buyer pays cash or uses a loan. Estate fiduciaries who never lived in the home are one listed exception.

Can I sell a Lincoln house that has a short-term rental license?

You can sell it, but the license is issued per rental unit and renewed annually at $250, so the buyer will need to sort out their own license status with the city's Planning and Development Services.

Where is Bellevue, Nebraska, and how big has it grown?

Bellevue is a Sarpy County city that the Nebraska State Historical Society calls the state's oldest community, and it now has more than 64,000 residents. The Census Bureau counted 50,137 residents in 2010 and 64,176 in 2020.

The city also grew in area. The Census Bureau lists the city's land area at 15.85 square miles in 2010 and 21.13 square miles in 2020, with about 3,037 people per square mile in 2020. A house on the newer edge of town can therefore be in a very different neighborhood from one near the old center, even though both carry a Bellevue address.

The 2025 estimate of 64,863 is slightly below the 2020 census base of 65,059, so the Census Bureau's numbers show the city roughly level since the 2020 count.

How did Bellevue begin?

Bellevue began around 1822 as a fur-trading post, and it later became the headquarters of a federal Indian agency. According to the State Historical Society's article Bellevue: The First Twenty Years, the post was set up by the Missouri Fur Company under Joshua Pilcher, then passed to Lucien Fontenelle and later to Peter A. Sarpy.

The agency for the Omaha, Pawnee, Oto and Missouri peoples moved to Bellevue in 1832. Missionaries and later Mormon, Oregon and California-bound travelers passed through, and the town came close to being chosen as the territorial capital.

What does Offutt Air Force Base mean for Bellevue home sellers?

Offutt Air Force Base, which MilitaryINSTALLATIONS ties to the Bellevue area, is the largest employer influence on the local economy. The same listing counts a combined military and civilian workforce of roughly 12,000 and more than 22,000 family members.

It also says the 2019 flood destroyed about a third of the base, roughly $700 million of property, and that the rebuild of the southeastern portion was scheduled to wrap up around 2027.

Military households move on orders rather than on a seller's preferred timeline. A Bellevue owner who gets reassigned, inherits a house, or cannot rent it out may need a fast close that does not depend on a buyer's loan approval.

Which public schools serve Bellevue?

Bellevue Public Schools is the main district, and it describes itself as serving about 10,000 students. The district lists two high schools, three middle schools, 15 elementary schools, one alternative school and a career and technical education center for pre-kindergarten through grade 12.

It operates as part of Sarpy County and Educational Service Unit 3. Buyers with children will often ask which elementary and middle school a specific address feeds, so a seller should have the exact street address ready and confirm attendance areas with the district rather than guess.

What does Bellevue's housing code say about a house in poor condition?

Chapter 15 of the Bellevue Code of Ordinances gives the Permits and Inspections Department authority to inspect dwellings and to placard a dwelling as unfit for human habitation. A seller with a damaged or neglected property should know that process, because it affects both value and timing.

  • Section 15-21 lets the department enter and inspect dwellings at reasonable times, and owners or occupants must give access.
  • Section 15-24 gives a person who receives a notice ten days to file a written petition for a hearing. Without a petition the notice automatically becomes an order.
  • Section 15-29 lists the defects that support an unfit placard, including a dwelling that is dilapidated, unsanitary, difficult to heat, unsafe or vermin infested.
  • Section 15-34 bars a placarded home from being lived in again until the department removes the placard in writing.
  • Section 15-36 prohibits gas or electric service to a placarded dwelling except for authorized repairs.
  • Section 15-37 creates a five-member Board of Housing Appeals to hear appeals from department decisions.

The city's Code Enforcement Unit enforces city codes and zoning ordinances in Bellevue and its zoning jurisdiction. Under section 15-35, tenants of a placarded building owe no rent from the date the placard goes up, so an owner with renters should move quickly on any notice.

How do Sarpy County valuation and tax offices affect a Bellevue sale?

Bellevue property tax is billed by Sarpy County, so the county's Treasurer, Assessor and Clerk, not city hall, are the offices a seller deals with. The Sarpy County Treasurer's Office is in the 1102 Building at 1102 E. 1st Street in Papillion and warns that wait times peak between 11:00 a.m. and 2:00 p.m., all day Fridays, and on the first and last day of any month.

The 2026 valuation protest period ran June 1 through June 30. Owners whose value changed received a goldenrod yellow postcard. A protest used Form 422 filed with the County Clerk at 1210 Golden Gate Drive in Papillion, in person by 4:45 p.m. on June 30, online by 11:59 p.m., or by mail postmarked by June 30. The county also cautions that a postal drop-box does not guarantee a same-day postmark, so mail should be postmarked in person at a post office.

Sarpy County's notice for 2025 gave the same June 1 through June 30 window, so a seller who thinks a value is too high before listing should plan for the June window rather than the closing date.

What does a Bellevue seller pay at closing?

A Bellevue seller pays Nebraska's documentary stamp tax on the deed, set by section 76-901 at $3.32 per $1,000 of value for transfers before January 1, 2032. On a $247,000 sale, the figure shown by Census for a median-value home, that tax would be $820.04 (247 thousands at $3.32).

Nebraska law also requires a written condition statement from sellers of one-to-four-unit homes under section 76-2,120, covering appliances, electrical, heating and cooling, water, sewer, hazardous conditions and title issues such as easements. The seller has to update it before the buyer is bound if something changes.

  • Gather a payoff letter for any mortgage or lien.
  • Ask the title company how the current year's property tax will be split.
  • Pull the written condition statement together before any buyer asks.

Sarpy County. Bellevue property tax is billed and collected by the Sarpy County Treasurer in Papillion, and valuation protests are filed with the Sarpy County Clerk.

Can the city of Bellevue condemn a house in bad shape?

Yes, through a defined process. Under Chapter 15 of the city code, the Permits and Inspections Department can placard a dwelling as unfit, serve a notice of intent to condemn, and report to the city council. An owner can petition for a hearing within ten days of a notice.

How much is Nebraska deed stamp tax on a Bellevue sale?

The seller pays $3.32 for each $1,000 of value, or fraction of $1,000, for transfers before January 1, 2032. A $200,000 sale would owe $664.

When is the property valuation protest deadline in Sarpy County?

The protest period runs June 1 through June 30 each year. Form 422 goes to the Sarpy County Clerk, in person by 4:45 p.m. on June 30, online by 11:59 p.m., or by mail postmarked on or before June 30.

It shapes the buyer and seller pool, since the base employs roughly 12,000 people according to MilitaryINSTALLATIONS. This page does not state a sale speed, because no official source publishes one for Bellevue.

Where is Grand Island, Nebraska, and how did it start?

Grand Island is the county seat of Hall County, in central Nebraska a few miles north of the Platte River, at about 1,870 feet in elevation. At the 2020 census it was the fourth-largest city in the state.

The name comes from a river island that French traders called La Grande Isle. In 1857, 35 German settlers from Davenport, Iowa, reached it on July 4 and built housing from local timber. The Union Pacific later laid out Grand Island Station slightly inland. The railroad arrived in 1868, and the town incorporated in 1872 (Wikipedia).

The metropolitan area takes in Hall, Hamilton, Howard and Merrick counties and had about 76,479 residents in a 2023 estimate.

What happened in the 1980 tornadoes, and why do buyers still ask about storms?

On June 3, 1980, a supercell hit Grand Island and produced seven tornadoes, the worst rated F4, and five people died. The north Locust business district took the heaviest damage.

Debris that could not be recycled was buried in Ryder Park and J. Dibbern Park, and the resulting mound, now called Tornado Hill, stands about 40 feet high. Local children use it for sledding.

Storm damage is part of local memory here. If your house has had hail or wind repairs, keep the paperwork. Nebraska's seller disclosure form asks about the condition of improvements, and a record of past repairs helps you answer honestly.

What is the weather like in Grand Island, and what does it do to a house?

Grand Island averages about 26.6 inches of precipitation and 27.7 inches of snow a year, based on 1991 to 2020 normals from the Central Nebraska Regional Airport. May is the wettest month at 4.70 inches. Records run from minus 34 degrees to 117 degrees.

May and June bring the most rain, so drainage deserves attention. Look at grading near the foundation, sump pumps, window wells and crawl spaces before a buyer's inspector does. Figures come from the climate table on Wikipedia.

Who employs people in Grand Island?

Manufacturing, agriculture, health care and logistics carry the local economy. The Grand Island Area Chamber of Commerce names six target sectors: transload and logistics, distribution and warehouse, manufacturing, agriculture and agribusiness, alternative energy, and data and call centers (Grand Island Area Chamber). Its economic development arm says Hornady and Chief Industries are among the companies with Grand Island locations that compete globally.

  • CHI Health St. Francis says it is a regional referral center with more than 1,100 employees and more than 100 physicians.
  • The Nebraska Law Enforcement Training Center, which trains officers for the whole state, is located here.
  • The Nebraska State Fair relocated to Grand Island, according to Wikipedia's summary of recent changes.

More than 140 freight trains a day pass through on Union Pacific, BNSF and Nebraska Central lines, so the freight network is a visible part of local life, and a house near the tracks may draw questions from buyers.

How do you get around Grand Island, and how far is the interstate?

Interstate 80 runs about 4 miles south of the city. U.S. 30 runs east and west through the center, and U.S. 281 is the main north-south route on the west edge. Central Nebraska Regional Airport is in town.

Grand Island has no fixed-route public transit. As of 2023 it was the largest city in Nebraska without it, and the local system is entirely demand-responsive with rides booked 24 hours ahead. The city also has fifteen traffic circles, many close together.

With no fixed-route bus, daily life here runs on cars. When you describe your house to any buyer, mention garage space, driveway width and the distance to Highway 281 or I-80.

Which school district covers Grand Island homes?

All of the city is in Grand Island Public Schools, and Grand Island Senior High School is its comprehensive high school. Private options include Central Catholic High School and Heartland Lutheran High School.

One detail trips up some buyers. Northwest Public Schools has a facility, including Northwest High School, inside Grand Island city limits, but none of that district's taxing and attendance boundary covers any part of the city. Property near the edge of town can sit in a different district, so check the district on the county tax statement rather than relying on the street address. Central Community College and the University of Nebraska at Kearney also serve the area.

What city rules apply when a Grand Island house is in poor condition?

Grand Island's code lets the Chief Building Official order an owner to make a dangerous building safe, and it requires written notice by first-class and certified mail to the owner of record. That process sits in the city's abatement of unsafe buildings article, and a separate Property Maintenance Code covers substandard conditions such as litter, weeds, debris and other hazards on the premises (Grand Island City Code).

  • Building Services covers the city and a two-mile area around it, and it enforces the 2021 International Residential Code with local amendments.
  • Inspections are scheduled at (308) 385-5325.
  • Rental owners must supply, install, maintain and test smoke detectors under the city code.

If you hold a house with open code issues, ask the city what is outstanding before you set a price. A cash buyer will account for the work. A financed buyer's lender may not accept the house until it is fixed. Information from the City of Grand Island Building Services page.

How are deeds and property tax handled in Hall County?

Hall County records deeds through the Register of Deeds, whose page lists the County Assessor as its contact, at 200 South Sycamore Street, Suite 6. Every deed that is recorded must come with the Real Estate Transfer Statement, Form 521, and the county's GIS viewer shows ownership and sale history for each parcel (Hall County Register of Deeds).

The county's published tax calendar gives these dates:

  • January 1: real property is assessed.
  • June 1: the assessor mails notices of valuation changes.
  • June 30: deadline for a protest and for a homestead exemption application.
  • October 15: levy date.
  • December 31: taxes are due. For a county with fewer than 100,000 people, the first half is delinquent May 1 and the second half September 1.

The Hall County Treasurer, at Suite 2 of the same building, also publishes a delinquent tax list each year. The state documentary stamp tax on the seller is $3.32 per $1,000 for deeds recorded from July 18, 2026 (Nebraska Department of Revenue).

What must a Grand Island seller put in the disclosure statement?

Nebraska Revised Statute 76-2,120 requires the statement to describe the condition of appliances that stay with the house, the electrical, heating, cooling, water and sewer systems, hazardous conditions, title matters such as easements and encroachments, utility connections, and compliance with carbon monoxide alarm rules. Any private transfer fee obligation must also be disclosed.

The statute lets you mark an item unknown if you truly do not know. It also protects a seller from liability for errors outside personal knowledge. What it does not allow is hiding something you know about. If a buyer does not receive the statement, they can recover damages, costs and attorney's fees (Nebraska Legislature).

When are Hall County property taxes due and delinquent?

Taxes are due December 31. Under the county's calendar for counties under 100,000 people, the first half is delinquent on May 1 and the second half on September 1.

What is the deadline to protest a Hall County valuation?

June 30 is the deadline for an individual real property protest, and the assessor sends valuation change notices by June 1.

Is Grand Island's whole city in one school district?

Yes. The city lies within Grand Island Public Schools, although a Northwest Public Schools facility sits inside the city limits without the district's taxing boundary covering any of it.

Can I sell a Grand Island house that has code violations?

Yes. Owners can sell with open issues, but the city can still send a written notice to the owner of record, so find out what is outstanding and tell the buyer in writing.

Who pays the Nebraska deed tax when a house is sold in Grand Island?

The grantor, meaning the seller, pays the documentary stamp tax. For deeds recorded from July 18, 2026, the rate is $3.32 per $1,000 of value, collected by the Hall County Register of Deeds.

Where did Kearney, Nebraska, come from?

Kearney grew up beside the Platte River on the trails west, and it is the county seat of Buffalo County. In 1848 the Army built Fort Kearny a few miles southeast of today's city to protect westbound travelers. The first permanent settlement, Dobytown, stood about two miles from the present downtown, and the extra "e" in the city's name is said to have come from postal clerks who kept misspelling it.

The Union Pacific arrived in 1866, a junction with the Burlington and Missouri River Railroad was fixed in 1871, and Kearney incorporated on December 3, 1873. A year later it became the county seat. The boom that followed produced an irrigation canal, an electric street railway and a five-story opera house, and it ended with the economic crisis of the early 1890s (Wikipedia).

Buffalo County's own Register of Deeds history adds a local detail: the first courthouse stood in Gibbon in 1873, and the records were moved to Kearney at night in a wagon. The first deed recorded in the county dates to February 12, 1870.

How big is Kearney, and how does the highway shape it?

Kearney covers about 13 square miles and sits on Interstate 80, with the Great Platte River Road Archway Monument spanning the highway at mile marker 274. The Census Bureau estimates 34,782 residents as of July 1, 2025, as noted at the top of this page.

The Union Pacific main line also runs through town, and the city operates Kearney Regional Airport east of the city.

The monument's exhibits trace the Great Platte River Road from the Oregon Trail days to the present, which fits a city that began as a stop for travelers. The county reports an average commute of 16 minutes, so when you describe a house to a buyer, give the minutes to the interstate and to the university.

Health care, education, retail and manufacturing anchor the Kearney economy. Buffalo County economic development reports 34,349 employed residents, an average commute of 16 minutes, and these top employers (Grow Buffalo County):

How does the University of Nebraska at Kearney affect local housing?

UNK is a 235-acre residential campus with more than 37 buildings, and it is among the largest employers in the city. It began in 1905 as the Nebraska State Normal School at Kearney, became a teachers college in 1921, was called Kearney State College from 1963 to 1991, and joined the University of Nebraska system in 1991.

  • Central Community College also has a branch campus in Kearney.
  • Kearney Public Schools runs three preschools, ten elementary schools, two middle schools and Kearney High School, and Kearney Catholic High School is the Catholic option.

If your house is tenant-occupied, give a buyer copies of the leases and the security deposit amounts early, so there are no surprises at closing.

What is the weather in Kearney, and what does it do to a house?

Kearney averages 25.56 inches of precipitation and 21.8 inches of snow a year, based on 1991 to 2020 NOAA normals for a station four miles northeast of town. The record high is 114 degrees and the record low is minus 30.

May is the wettest month at 4.40 inches, with June next at 3.90. Snow falls mainly from November to March, with February the snowiest at 5.6 inches. Hot summers and cold, dry winters stress roofing, siding and concrete flatwork, and a buyer's inspector will note all three.

If your house needs a roof or a furnace, get a written bid before you decide how to sell. It gives you a real number to weigh against a cash offer, rather than a guess.

What do Kearney's Development Services and code enforcement handle?

Kearney's Development Services Department combines permit services, code enforcement, inspections and planning and zoning in one place. Building Services administers the adopted zoning, building, electrical and plumbing codes, and Code Enforcement takes complaints at (308) 233-3235 or through the Access Kearney app (City of Kearney).

  • Because Building Services inspects work against the adopted building, electrical and plumbing codes, ask whether past projects on your house were permitted.
  • Residents can file a code complaint by phone or through the Access Kearney app.
  • Ask the department for open permits or violations on your address before you accept an offer.

We did not find a Kearney rule that requires an inspection or certificate when a single-family house is sold. The city code is on Municode if you want to read the chapters yourself.

How do Buffalo County deed recording and taxes work?

The Buffalo County Register of Deeds, Jen Schleusener since February 2026, records deeds in the courthouse in Kearney from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. on weekdays, and copies cost $0.50 a page. The office warns about a "Recorded Deed Notice" mail scam that asks for $86 and says to send no money. It also offers a free Property Fraud Alert that emails or texts you when a document is recorded under your name (Buffalo County Register of Deeds).

The Register of Deeds is a separate office in counties with more than 20,000 inhabitants. The same page says the state documentary stamp tax rises from $2.32 to $3.32 per $1,000 under LB1067, beginning July 18, 2026 and ending December 31, 2031. A seller pays it when the deed is recorded, so on a $250,000 house the tax is $830.

Property taxes are billed by the Buffalo County Treasurer, Brenda Rohrich, at PO Box 1270, Kearney, phone (308) 236-1250. The Treasurer's page lists tax sales among its services. Hall County's published calendar cites statute 77-204 for May 1 and September 1 delinquency in counties under 100,000 people, so ask the Treasurer to confirm the exact dates for your parcel.

What must a Kearney seller do about the disclosure form and its timing?

The disclosure statement must reach the buyer on or before the effective date of the binding contract, and the buyer must acknowledge receipt in writing. If you learn something before that date that makes the statement wrong, you must update it.

Plan for this early. Fill the form out at the start, not after you accept an offer. It covers appliances, the electrical, heating and cooling, water and sewer systems, defects that affect value, hazardous substances, title conditions and carbon monoxide alarm compliance (Nebraska Legislature).

A missed form does not void the transfer. The buyer can still sue for actual damages and attorney's fees, so complete it every time.

The Buffalo County Register of Deeds, located in the county courthouse in Kearney. Call (308) 236-1239 or email deeds@buffalocounty.ne.gov.

What is the Nebraska documentary stamp tax rate for a Kearney sale?

It is $3.32 per $1,000 of value from July 18, 2026. The Buffalo County notice says the increase runs through December 31, 2031.

What is the Recorded Deed Notice scam in Buffalo County?

It is a mailer that asks for about $86 for a copy of a recorded deed. The Register of Deeds says copies cost $0.50 a page at the courthouse and that people should not send money.

Does Kearney require a point-of-sale inspection for a house?

We did not find one for single-family homes in the city pages we reviewed. Call Kearney Development Services at the number on the city's code enforcement page to confirm.

Kearney Public Schools, which operates preschools, ten elementary schools, two middle schools and Kearney High School.

Where is Fremont, Nebraska, and how large is it?

Fremont is the county seat of Dodge County in eastern Nebraska, and the Nebraska Association of County Officials puts its 2025 population at 28,350. The 2020 census count was 27,141, which Wikipedia notes made it the sixth most populous city in the state.

The city covers about 10.8 square miles of land, and the county tracks Platte River flows at a gauge near Fremont. Wikipedia reports that it was founded in 1856, incorporated on June 17, 1871, and named for the U.S. general and politician John C. Fremont.

Fremont Lakes State Recreation Area, a cluster of man-made lakes along the north bank of the Platte, covers 667 acres in Dodge County according to the county fact sheet.

Fremont dwarfs the rest of Dodge County. The fact sheet lists North Bend at 1,263 residents, Scribner at 814, Hooper at 793 and six villages, and counts 5,085 people, 13 percent of the county, in unincorporated areas. The county also reports 2,310 veterans in 2026.

How did Dodge County and Fremont get started?

Fremont grew up to serve traffic on the Platte River and the Mormon Trail, and it won the county seat in a special election in 1860. Dodge County was organized in 1855 and named for Senator Augustus Dodge, the Iowa senator who introduced the bill that became the Kansas-Nebraska Act.

Early settlers were trappers, traders and hunters, followed by farm families. The county fact sheet says Dodge County grew by nearly 20,000 residents between 1860 and 1890. The first courthouse went up in 1867 on donated land, a new one replaced it in 1890, and the present courthouse was built after a fire in 1915.

Dodge County has 22 registered historic places in all. Historic downtown Fremont is listed on the National Register of Historic Places, and the city holds John C. Fremont Days each July. Both facts come from Wikipedia, which also notes that the Louis E. May Historical Museum occupies a Victorian house built in 1874 by Fremont's first mayor, Theron Nye.

What keeps the Fremont economy going?

Meatpacking, health care, schools and agriculture have long been the biggest employers in Fremont. A Greater Fremont Development Council list from 2016, cited by Wikipedia, put Hormel Foods first with an estimated 1,000 to 1,500 workers, followed by Fremont Health Medical Center, Fremont Public Schools and Nye Health Services at 500 to 1,000 each. Those are 2016 estimates, so check current numbers with the council.

Wikipedia also reports that Costco began building a poultry complex in Fremont in 2019, with a processing facility, hatchery and feed mill known as Lincoln Premium Poultry.

Fremont Public Schools is one of the five school districts listed for Dodge County, and Midland University is the city's four-year college. The other districts on the county list are Howells-Dodge Consolidated, Logan View, Scribner-Snyder and West Point Public Schools.

Midland describes more than 140 years of history and a campus in the heart of Fremont, and the county places Dodge County in the Metropolitan Community College service area.

Which Dodge County offices handle property tax?

The Assessor, Treasurer and Register of Deeds work at the Dodge County Courthouse, 435 N Park Avenue in Fremont. The fact sheet lists courthouse hours of 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Monday through Friday, and the county board meets every other Wednesday.

  • Assessor: Brandy Marshall, Room 202, 402-727-3911. The assessor's site lists hours of 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.
  • Treasurer: mail to PO Box 999, Fremont, NE 68026. The line for real estate and personal property taxes is 402-727-2750.
  • Register of Deeds: records the deed after a sale.

The county fact sheet shows a county levy of $0.221 per $100, $14,727,024 of county property tax and $89,875,353 across all local governments, on taxable valuation of $6,311,522,302. That puts the county's own share near 16 percent. On a $200,000 valuation the county levy would be $442, with schools, the city and other districts adding to it.

What utilities and land rules affect a Fremont sale?

Dodge County is listed as a zoned county, and the Lower Elkhorn and Lower Platte North natural resource districts both reach into it. The county counts 726 rural drinking water wells, 1,745 irrigation and livestock wells, and 111 surface water diversions for irrigation.

The county also links live stream gauges for the Platte River at North Bend and near Fremont, along with Logan Creek and Maple Creek. The county owns 264 bridges and one dam, so the condition of the county road that serves an acreage is a fair question to raise early. A seller on acreage near a stream should expect questions from buyers and lenders about flood history and be ready with answers.

Under section 76-2,120, the seller must hand over a signed condition statement by the time a contract binds the buyer, and must correct it if something changes beforehand. Court-ordered transfers, foreclosure sales and transfers to a spouse or lineal relative are among the listed exceptions.

Because of that road pattern, a house near 13th Street or Omaha Avenue is a quick drive to everything else in town, which helps when buyers are comparing blocks.

How did Norfolk begin, and what does that mean for older houses?

Norfolk was founded by German Lutheran settlers from near Ixonia, Wisconsin, who sent scouts west in late 1865 looking for farmland they could claim under the Homestead Act. A party of 124 people from 42 families set out in May 1866 and reached the site on July 15.

Railroads turned the settlement into a town. The Fremont, Elkhorn and Missouri Valley line arrived in 1879, the Union Pacific branch from Columbus in 1880, and the Chicago, St. Paul, Minneapolis and Omaha line in 1882. Norfolk passed 1,000 residents in 1886, and a public water supply and street railway followed in 1887.

The census counts show how fast the town grew afterward: 3,883 people in 1900, 8,634 in 1920 and 10,717 in 1930. Much of the older housing near the center probably dates from those decades, so sellers of early twentieth century homes often deal with original wiring, plumbing and foundations that a buyer financing with a mortgage will want inspected.

What weather and flood risk should a Norfolk seller plan for?

Norfolk has a continental climate with hot summers and cold, snowy winters. At the airport weather station, the 1991 to 2020 normals show about 27 inches of precipitation and nearly 30 inches of snowfall in a typical year, and the all-time record high there is 116 degrees Fahrenheit.

Those numbers point to the parts of a house a buyer will look at first: the roof and gutters after winter loads and summer storms, the furnace and insulation, and the air conditioning. A house with an aging roof or a furnace near the end of its life is the kind of property where a seller often weighs a repair bill against an as-is sale.

The Elkhorn River adds a second question. The 2019 flood event damaged the city levees, and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers awarded a $2.69 million contract on April 22, 2020 to repair the damaged Norfolk Elkhorn River levee projects on the left and right banks, with work scheduled to start in June 2020 and finish by February 2021. If a property is in a mapped flood zone, the lender will require flood insurance, and a buyer will ask for the cost. The National Weather Service posts live river readings for the Elkhorn at Norfolk, and the Nebraska Department of Natural Resources runs the state floodplain program.

What city rules can slow down a Norfolk house sale?

The most common snag is a nuisance notice under Chapter 17 of the Norfolk Municipal Code, which covers weeds, litter and vehicles on private property. Cleaning these up before a sale, or settling them with the buyer, keeps a closing from stalling.

  • Weeds and noxious growth count as a nuisance once they pass 12 inches in height.
  • Inoperable, wrecked or unregistered vehicles may not stay on a property longer than 30 days unless they are inside an enclosed building.
  • The city serves notice by personal delivery or certified mail. If the owner does not ask for a hearing or comply within five days of receipt, the city can do the work and assess the cost against the lot like a special tax.
  • The city adds an administrative fee of $25 to weed, litter and drainage billings.

Building permits follow the fee schedule in Section 2-5 of the code. As of the October 2025 update, new construction and additions cost $0.26 per finished square foot above grade and $0.18 per square foot for basements, a basement finish or remodel is $0.215 per square foot, the minimum permit is $36.25 and a demolition permit is $54. Starting work before applying triples the permit fee. A seller who finished a basement without a permit should expect the question to come up in a buyer's inspection.

How does a deed transfer work in Madison County?

A Norfolk sale is recorded with the Madison County Register of Deeds, and the deed must be accompanied by a Real Estate Transfer Statement, Form 521, from the Nebraska Department of Revenue. The county posts a recording schedule that starts at $10 for a one-page document, $16 for two pages and $22 for three, rising $6 for each added page.

The state documentary stamp tax is the larger number. The Department of Revenue says the rate is $3.32 for each $1,000 of value, or fraction of that, for deeds recorded on or after July 18, 2026, and it is imposed on the grantor who signs the deed. On a sale price of $200,000, that works out to $664, though some transfers are exempt. Check the department's exemption list if the deed is between family members or comes from an estate.

Property tax is separate. Madison County real and personal property taxes are due December 31, with the first half delinquent on the following May 1 and the second half on September 1. Nebraska sets interest on delinquent political subdivision taxes at 14 percent a year. At a closing, the title company usually prorates the current year's tax between buyer and seller, so ask for the figure before you sign.

Which schools and colleges serve Norfolk homes?

Norfolk Public Schools is the public district, with elementary schools, one junior high, Norfolk Senior High and an alternative high school, and enrollment above 4,000 according to the most recent summary on file. Norfolk Catholic Schools and several Lutheran schools add private options.

Northeast Community College is based in Norfolk and is a steady source of both students and jobs. Families relocating for a job at Faith Regional or one of the plants often start their search by school attendance area, so it helps to state the elementary school on any listing or offer summary. Our team does not rate schools, and a family should confirm boundaries with the district before relying on an address.

What do sellers in Norfolk usually face, and where does a cash sale fit?

Most Norfolk sellers who contact a cash buyer are dealing with one of a few situations: an inherited house that no one lives in, a rental with a tenant or a turnover problem, a house with deferred repairs, or a move that has a hard date. Each one has a local wrinkle. An inherited house may need to clear probate through Nebraska's county court before a deed can be signed. A rental needs lease terms checked. A house with a nuisance notice needs the weeds, vehicles or litter dealt with or assigned in writing.

A cash sale removes the lender from the transaction, so appraisal and loan approval no longer set the closing date. The seller still signs a deed, the Madison County recording steps above still apply, and a title company still confirms that taxes and liens are cleared. If you want to compare routes, ask for a written offer and weigh it against a list-and-repair plan with your own numbers. You owe nothing to hear what a cash offer looks like.

The Nebraska Department of Revenue lists the documentary stamp tax at $3.32 for each $1,000 of value for deeds recorded on or after July 18, 2026. On a $150,000 sale that is $498, unless an exemption applies. The Madison County Register of Deeds collects it when the deed is recorded.

When are Madison County property taxes due?

Real estate taxes are due December 31. The first half becomes delinquent the following May 1 and the second half on September 1, with 14 percent annual interest on late amounts under Nebraska law. Confirm balances with the Madison County Treasurer before closing.

Can the city of Norfolk bill me for yard or vehicle problems?

Yes. Under Chapter 17 of the municipal code, if you do not request a hearing or fix a nuisance within five days of receiving notice, the city can abate it and assess the cost against the property like a special tax. Weeds over 12 inches and vehicles inoperable for more than 30 days are covered.

Does Norfolk have flood risk that affects a sale?

Parts of the city lie along the Elkhorn River, whose 2019 flood event damaged levees and led to a $2.69 million Army Corps repair contract. A buyer's lender may require flood insurance if the property is in a mapped flood zone, so check the flood map for the address early.

Where is Columbus, Nebraska, and what is it known for?

Columbus is the seat of Platte County in east-central Nebraska, at the meeting point of the Loup and Platte rivers. Platte County's own history page says the Columbus Town Company sent agents from Columbus, Ohio in the summer of 1856, and that they marked the townsite when they reached the Loup River. The settlement soon had a mill, a hotel and a general store.

Inside the county, Columbus is by far the largest place. The NACO fact sheet gives it 24,028 residents in 2020 as a first-class city, against 905 in Humphrey and 667 in Newman Grove, and puts 23 percent of county residents outside any incorporated town. The county board meets every other Tuesday.

The county board's share is therefore about 15 percent of the total. On a $200,000 valuation the county levy alone comes to $369.20, and schools, the city and other districts add to that.

Because Columbus sits where two rivers meet, a seller should expect buyers to ask about flood exposure. The county's online map viewer includes basemap layers labeled 2019 Flood and 2020 Flood.

The county fact sheet lists four natural resource districts with territory in Platte County: Central Platte, Lower Elkhorn, Lower Loup and Lower Platte North. It counts 1,297 rural drinking water wells and 2,150 irrigation wells. Any well capable of more than 50 gallons a minute must be registered and permitted through the local district.

The same fact sheet marks Platte County as not zoned, so county-level zoning does not apply outside the incorporated towns. City zoning and building permits still apply inside Columbus.

What does a Columbus seller owe at closing?

A Columbus seller owes Nebraska's documentary stamp tax, calculated under section 76-901 at $3.32 per $1,000 for transfers before 2032 and $2.32 after that. On a $200,000 sale the tax is $664.

Sellers of homes with up to four units also complete the written disclosure that section 76-2,120 requires, listing the condition of electrical, heating, water, sewer and other systems as the seller knows them. Through public power. The county fact sheet lists Cornhusker Public Power District, Elkhorn Rural Public Power District and Loup River Public Power District as providers in Platte County.

How did Hastings, Nebraska, get its housing stock?

Hastings was founded in 1872 where two railroads crossed, and its houses still show the booms and busts that followed. It was named for Colonel D. T. Hastings, who helped bring the railroad through Adams County. The city incorporated in April 1874, and in 1878 it won the county seat from Juniata after a five-year dispute (Wikipedia).

A fire in 1879 destroyed 33 downtown buildings, and the city was rebuilt between 1880 and 1890 in fireproof materials. Growth stalled in the 1890s, then returned from 1900 to 1930, which left Craftsman, Prairie, Colonial Revival and American Foursquare houses. By 1911 Hastings made more bricks than any other Nebraska city.

Heartwell Park and Central Hastings, two of the oldest neighborhoods, are on the National Register of Historic Places. If you own a home in either, ask the city about any review that applies before you plan exterior work.

What did the Naval Ammunition Depot do to Hastings housing?

The Naval Ammunition Depot, built in 1942, caused a housing shortage that reshaped parts of the city. Hastings grew from about 15,000 to 23,000 people in under a year, which led to alterations of existing houses and rapid construction of new neighborhoods. An 840-unit village called Spencer Park was built for workers.

When the war ended, depot staffing shrank, and the depot eventually closed. Central Community College now occupies buildings from the former depot. In 2023 the National Park Service named Hastings an American World War II Heritage City because of the depot.

  • Some Hastings houses date to this wartime building push, and others were altered to take in workers.
  • Homes of that age may still have original wiring, plumbing or windows.
  • Buyers who finance may need repairs finished before a lender will fund.

Where does Hastings sit, and what is the climate?

Hastings is the county seat of Adams County, covers about 13.7 square miles, and lies roughly 14 miles south of Interstate 80. U.S. 6, U.S. 34 and U.S. 281 meet the city, and Amtrak's California Zephyr stops here once a day in each direction. The city owns Hastings Municipal Airport.

A National Weather Service forecast office in Hastings covers central and south-central Nebraska and six counties in north-central Kansas. The 1991 to 2020 normals show 26.54 inches of precipitation and 28.4 inches of snow a year, with records from minus 30 to 116 degrees.

What drives jobs and growth in Hastings?

The Hastings Economic Development Corporation, formed in 1973, develops industrial parks, helps businesses expand and works to attract new employers. The city describes itself as near the geographic center of the United States (City of Hastings).

Mary Lanning Healthcare says it is the largest employer in Adams County. The Census Bureau's 2023 QuickFacts for Adams County counts 989 employer establishments and 12,926 people in employer jobs (Census Bureau). Hastings College, founded in 1882, and Central Community College, which opened in 1966, add education jobs.

Hastings Public Schools is the school district. The public high school is Hastings High School, and Adams Central Junior-Senior High School sits just outside town. St. Cecilia's is the Catholic high school.

The Kool-Aid story is part of local identity too. Edwin Perkins invented the powder in Hastings in 1927, and the town hosts Kool-Aid Days on the second weekend of August.

How do Adams County offices handle deeds and property tax?

The Adams County Register of Deeds records deeds at 500 N. Denver Avenue, and recorded documents can be returned within 24 hours because they are scanned daily. The Treasurer, in Suite 106 of the courthouse at 500 West 4th Street, bills real estate taxes on December 1 each year. They are due December 31. First-half taxes are delinquent on May 1 of the next year and second-half taxes on September 1 (Adams County Treasurer).

The Treasurer's office also notes that replats are signed only after the current year's taxes are paid in full, and it runs public and private tax sales for unpaid taxes.

What does a Hastings seller owe a buyer in writing?

A Hastings seller of a house with one to four units must hand the buyer a written disclosure statement signed by the seller, no later than the effective date of a binding purchase contract. The statute also says the seller must update the statement if something on it becomes inaccurate before then.

A seller is not liable for an error that was outside personal knowledge, and agents are not liable unless they knew. That is why honest answers, including "unknown," matter so much. Under Nebraska Revised Statute 76-2,120, a lawsuit over a missing statement must start within one year after the buyer takes possession or the conveyance, whichever comes first.
